questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless nodule on the dorsum of his right hand that ulcerated over 3 weeks. The lesion has a characteristic 'volcano crater' appearance with surrounding satellite nodules. Gram stain of pus shows Gram-positive filamentous organisms. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Nocardia brasiliensis causes actinomycetoma (mycetoma with Gram-positive filaments), common in farmers. It presents with triad: tumefaction, sinuses, and grains. Actinomyces israelii causes cervicofacial actinomycosis. Sporothrix causes sporotrichosis (fungal, not bacterial). M. marinum causes fish tank granuloma.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with pruritic, annular scaly plaques on her trunk. KOH mount shows fungal hyphae. She is started on oral terbinafine. After 2 weeks, she develops jaundice and elevated liver enzymes. What is the mechanism of terbinafine-induced hepatotoxicity?
opts: Inhibition of CYP3A4 leading to drug accumulation
Cholestasis due to bile salt pump inhibition
questions.exp: Terbinafine hepatotoxicity is an idiosyncratic immune-mediated reaction, not dose-dependent. It occurs in approximately 1:50,000 patients. Terbinafine inhibits CYP2D6 (not 3A4). Liver function tests should be monitored in patients on prolonged therapy. The reaction is not predictable from dose.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with multiple fluid-filled blisters on the face and hands, some of which are honey-crusted. Nikolsky sign is negative. Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus phage group II. Which toxin is responsible for the blister formation?
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo is caused by exfoliative toxins (ET-A and ET-B) produced by S. aureus phage group II. These toxins are serine proteases that cleave desmoglein-1 in the superficial epidermis (stratum granulosum), causing intraepidermal blistering. TSST-1 causes toxic shock syndrome. Alpha toxin causes cell lysis.

questions.q: A 24-year-old sexually active man presents with a painless genital ulcer with indurated margins and associated inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy shows motile spirochetes. Serological tests show RPR positive and TPHA positive. Which stage of syphilis is this?
questions.exp: Primary syphilis presents with a painless indurated ulcer (chancre) at the site of inoculation, accompanied by painless regional lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy shows Treponema pallidum. Both RPR (non-treponemal) and TPHA (treponemal) can be positive in primary syphilis. Secondary syphilis manifests with skin rashes, mucous patches, and condyloma lata.

questions.q: A 45-year-old leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden onset erythematous nodules on face and limbs, fever, and pain in hands. Nerve function is intact. This is classified as what type of lepra reaction?
questions.exp: Type 2 reaction (ENL) occurs in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It is an immune complex-mediated (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction presenting with painful erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic features. Nerve function is usually preserved unless neuritis develops. Type 1 (reversal reaction) involves nerve damage and is a Type IV hypersensitivity. Lucio phenomenon is a severe necrotizing vasculitis in Lucio leprosy.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with tense bullae arising on normal and erythematous skin, predominantly on flexures and inner thighs. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. ELISA is positive for anti-BP180 antibodies. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is characterized by tense subepidermal bullae on flexures, linear IgG and C3 at DEJ on DIF, and antibodies against BP180 (type XVII collagen) and BP230. It is the most common autoimmune blistering disorder. Pemphigus vulgaris shows flaccid blisters, intraepidermal splitting, IgG at cell surfaces (chicken-wire pattern). DIF shows IgA in DH; Linear IgA disease shows linear IgA at DEJ.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with malar erythema, discoid lesions, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, and non-scarring alopecia. ANA is positive at 1:640 with speckled pattern. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies are elevated. Which antibody is most specific for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibodies are highly specific (>99%) for SLE, though not very sensitive (25-30%). Anti-dsDNA is highly specific and correlates with disease activity and nephritis but is less specific than anti-Sm. Anti-Ro/SSA is associated with neonatal lupus and Sjogren's syndrome. Anti-histone antibodies are characteristically seen in drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasias on his nose that has been slowly growing for 2 years. Biopsy shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artifact. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Wide local excision with 2 cm margins
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma on the nose (H-zone) is best treated with Mohs micrographic surgery, which provides the highest cure rates (99%) with maximal tissue conservation. This is important for facial lesions where functional and cosmetic outcomes matter. Wide excision with 2 cm margins is for melanoma. Radiation is an option but inferior for H-zone BCC. Topical 5-FU is for superficial BCC only.

questions.q: A 40-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 150 cells/μL) presents with multiple purplish-red plaques on his lower limbs. Biopsy shows proliferation of spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces, and extravasated red blood cells. Which virus is implicated in the pathogenesis?
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by Human Herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi's Sarcoma-Associated Herpesvirus (KSHV). In HIV patients with low CD4 counts, epidemic KS manifests as purplish plaques on lower limbs. Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular channels, and haemosiderin deposits. Treatment includes HAART, local therapies (cryotherapy, radiotherapy), and systemic chemotherapy (liposomal doxorubicin).

questions.q: A patient started on phenytoin develops widespread erythematous macules that coalesce, with target lesions and blistering involving >30% BSA, along with mucous membrane erosions. The Nikolsky sign is positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) involves >30% BSA detachment (SJS: <10%, SJS/TEN overlap: 10-30%). It is most commonly drug-induced (phenytoin, sulfonamides, allopurinol). Nikolsky sign is positive. SSSS (Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome) affects children, occurs superficially (subcorneal cleavage), and is infection-induced. EM major is less severe and often herpes-triggered.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a dermatomal distribution along T5, associated with severe burning pain. He is treated with acyclovir. After the rash resolves, he continues to have severe pain at the same site for 3 months. What is this complication?
questions.exp: Post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) is defined as pain persisting beyond 3 months after the acute zoster rash. It is the most common complication of herpes zoster, more common in elderly patients. Treatment includes gabapentin, pregabalin, tricyclic antidepressants, and capsaicin. Early antiviral therapy reduces (but doesn't eliminate) the risk of PHN. Ramsay Hunt involves the geniculate ganglion with ear pain and facial palsy.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with multiple hypopigmented patches on her trunk with fine scales. Wood's lamp examination shows yellowish-green fluorescence. KOH mount shows 'spaghetti and meatball' appearance. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (now classified as M. globosa, M. sympodialis). KOH mount shows the characteristic 'spaghetti and meatball' pattern (hyphae + spores). Wood's lamp shows yellowish-green fluorescence. The organism is a commensal that becomes pathogenic under certain conditions (heat, humidity, immunosuppression). Treatment: topical/oral azoles, selenium sulfide.

questions.q: A 20-year-old patient with lepromatous leprosy is started on dapsone. After 2 weeks, he develops pallor, jaundice, and fatigue. His Hb drops to 7 g/dL. Peripheral smear shows Heinz bodies and bite cells. What is the mechanism?
questions.exp: Dapsone causes dose-dependent oxidative hemolysis due to generation of reactive metabolites (hydroxylamine). This is exaggerated in G6PD deficiency. Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin) and bite cells (macrophages removing Heinz bodies) are characteristic. Methemoglobinemia is another dose-dependent effect. Dapsone syndrome (idiosyncratic) includes rash, fever, lymphadenopathy, and hepatitis.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales on her elbows, knees, and scalp. She also has nail changes (pitting, onycholysis) and joint pain in her fingers. Which HLA type is most strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis?
questions.exp: HLA-B27 is strongly associated with psoriatic arthritis, particularly the axial (spondylitic) subtype. HLA-Cw6 is the most strongly associated with psoriasis vulgaris itself. HLA-B13 and HLA-B17 are also associated with psoriasis. HLA-B57 is associated with abacavir hypersensitivity reactions. The pathogenesis involves TNF-alpha, IL-17, and IL-23 pathways.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a single hypopigmented patch on his left cheek with loss of sensation. Slit skin smear is negative. Biopsy shows a well-formed granuloma in the dermis with very few AFB. Nerve fascicles are infiltrated but not destroyed. What is the leprosy type?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid (TT) leprosy presents with 1-5 well-defined hypopigmented anaesthetic patches. It is paucibacillary (SSS negative). Histology shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas that may touch or destroy nerve fibers (perineural granulomas). Lepromin test is strongly positive. It represents the high-resistance pole. Borderline tuberculoid (BT) has similar features but slightly more lesions and less clearly defined margins.

questions.q: A 19-year-old girl presents with comedones, papules, pustules, and nodules on her face and back. She has been using topical clindamycin for 6 months with inadequate response. She is started on isotretinoin. Which of the following is the most serious teratogenic effect of isotretinoin?
opts: Central nervous system and cardiac malformations
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen causing retinoic acid embryopathy. The most serious defects include CNS malformations (hydrocephalus, microcephaly), cardiac defects (transposition of great vessels, VSD), microtia/anotia, and micrognathia. It should be avoided in pregnancy (Category X). Adequate contraception is mandatory before, during, and 1 month after treatment. iPLEDGE program monitors compliance in the US.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope rash around the eyes, Gottron's papules over MCP joints, and V-sign erythema on the chest. CK is elevated at 3000 IU/L. Which antibody is associated with increased risk of interstitial lung disease in this condition?
questions.exp: Anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl-tRNA synthetase) is the most common anti-synthetase antibody in dermatomyositis/polymyositis. It is associated with the anti-synthetase syndrome: ILD, myositis, inflammatory arthritis, mechanic's hands, fever, and Raynaud's phenomenon. Anti-Mi-2 is associated with classic DM with good prognosis. Anti-SRP predicts severe necrotizing myopathy. Anti-p155/140 (TIF1-gamma) is associated with cancer-associated DM.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with a slowly enlarging, painless ulcer on his lower leg with undermined edges and a violaceous border. He has a history of Crohn's disease. Biopsy shows sterile neutrophilic infiltrate. Which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.exp: Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) is a neutrophilic dermatosis associated with IBD, rheumatoid arthritis, and hematological malignancies. Pathergy (worsening with trauma) is a key feature - surgical debridement is contraindicated as it worsens the ulcer. First-line treatment is systemic corticosteroids or cyclosporine. Biologic agents (infliximab) are used in refractory cases, especially in IBD-associated PG.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a rapidly growing, firm nodule on his ear that has developed over 6 weeks. The lesion has a central keratin-filled crater with overhanging edges. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma (KA) is a rapidly growing squamoproliferative tumor that typically develops over 4-8 weeks and may spontaneously regress over months. Clinically it presents as a dome-shaped nodule with a central keratin crater on sun-exposed skin. It is histologically similar to well-differentiated SCC and many experts consider it a variant of SCC. Treatment is excision. Merkel cell carcinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor with distinct histology.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with multiple painful oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. She also has a positive pathergy test. Which HLA type is most strongly associated with this condition?
questions.exp: Behcet's disease is strongly associated with HLA-B51, particularly in patients from the 'Silk Road' countries (Turkey, Middle East, East Asia). The classic triad includes recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. Pathergy (papule formation at skin puncture site) is a characteristic finding. Complications include ocular involvement leading to blindness, vascular (aneurysms, thrombosis), and CNS involvement.

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with widespread crusting of the scalp, face, and flexures. The mother reports the child has had eczema since infancy. Patch testing is negative. Serum IgE is markedly elevated. Filaggrin gene mutation is suspected. What role does filaggrin play in the skin?
opts: Promotes cornification and skin barrier function
questions.exp: Filaggrin (FLG) is a key structural protein in the stratum corneum that aggregates keratin filaments and is processed to natural moisturizing factor (NMF). Loss-of-function mutations in FLG impair the epidermal barrier, allowing allergen penetration and water loss, predisposing to atopic dermatitis. FLG mutations are the strongest genetic risk factor for AD. Tight junction integrity is maintained by claudins and occludins.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with linear streaks of erythema and vesicles on her forearm after working in the garden. The pattern follows lines of dripping fluid. What is the pathomechanism of this reaction?
opts: Direct cytotoxic reaction from plant sap
questions.exp: Phytophotodermatitis is a phototoxic (not allergic) reaction caused by furocoumarins (psoralens) from plants (Umbelliferae family: parsley, celery, fig, lime) activated by UVA. It presents with erythema, vesicles, and bullae in irregular streaks or drip patterns on sun-exposed areas, followed by post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. No prior sensitization is needed (unlike allergic contact dermatitis which is type IV). Treatment is symptomatic.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with pruritic, grouped vesicles on the elbows, knees, and buttocks. Skin biopsy shows subepidermal vesicles with neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillary tips. DIF shows granular IgA deposits at the DEJ. What is the associated systemic condition?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is strongly associated with coeliac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy) in virtually all patients. Granular IgA deposits at the DEJ on DIF are pathognomonic. Anti-endomysial (AEA) and anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTG) antibodies are elevated. Gluten-free diet is the primary treatment and improves both skin and gut disease. Dapsone provides symptomatic relief but does not treat the gut.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with thickened, warty, hyperpigmented plaques in the axillae and neck. He recently noticed rapid progression over 3 months. Laboratory investigations reveal high insulin-like growth factor levels. Which malignancy is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.exp: Malignant acanthosis nigricans (AN) is most commonly associated with gastric adenocarcinoma (50% of internal malignancy-associated AN). It develops rapidly in older patients without obesity. The pathomechanism involves TGF-alpha and IGF-1 binding to skin receptors. It is a paraneoplastic dermatosis. Benign AN is associated with insulin resistance, obesity, and endocrine disorders. The Triple AN (AN + tripe palms + acrochordons) strongly suggests malignancy.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman is undergoing electrosurgery for a seborrheic keratosis. She is wearing a pacemaker. What modification to the procedure is necessary?
opts: Use monopolar electrocautery with grounding pad on the thigh
Use bipolar electrocautery to minimize current spread
Increase the power setting to reduce procedure time
questions.exp: In patients with pacemakers, bipolar electrosurgery is preferred because the electrical current flows only between the two tips of the forceps, minimizing current spread that could interfere with the pacemaker. Monopolar electrocautery generates current that passes through the body to the grounding pad, risking interference with pacemakers and ICDs. Cardiology consultation and pacemaker reprogramming (to asynchronous mode) may also be necessary.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with progressive tightening of facial skin, difficulty opening the mouth, and Raynaud's phenomenon since 1 year. She has sclerodactyly and calcinosis. ANA is positive. Which antibody pattern is associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome)?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibodies (ACA) are associated with limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc/CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, oEsophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). ACA are specific (~95%) for lcSSc. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and predicts ILD and poor prognosis. Anti-RNA polymerase III predicts renal crisis in diffuse SSc. Anti-U1 RNP is seen in mixed connective tissue disease.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man presents with palpable purpura on his lower limbs. He has a recent history of upper respiratory infection. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits. Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein Purpura) is characterized by: palpable purpura (predominantly lower limbs), arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal involvement (IgA nephropathy). IgA deposits in vessel walls on DIF/biopsy are diagnostic. It often follows upper respiratory infection (streptococcal). Though more common in children, it occurs in adults with worse prognosis. GPA (Wegener's) has c-ANCA/PR3. MPA has p-ANCA/MPO.

questions.q: During a Tzanck smear preparation from a blister base, multinucleated giant cells with nuclear molding and 'ground glass' nuclei are seen. This finding is positive in which of the following conditions?
opts: Herpes simplex and herpes zoster only
Herpes simplex, herpes zoster, and varicella
questions.exp: Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells (acantholytic cells with nuclear molding, 'ground glass' nuclei, and peripheral chromatin margination) in all herpetic infections: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV (herpes zoster and varicella). It cannot distinguish between these. Pemphigus vulgaris shows acantholytic cells (Tzanck cells) but these are mononuclear, rounded cells without the giant cell features. The test is rapid, cheap, but lacks sensitivity and specificity.

questions.q: A 23-year-old man presents with a painless, firm papule on the glans penis that has been present for 3 weeks. He is sexually active and uses condoms inconsistently. The lesion has irregular margins and warty surface. PCR confirms HPV type 16. What is the risk associated with this HPV type?
opts: Penile intraepithelial neoplasia and invasive carcinoma
questions.exp: HPV type 16 is a high-risk oncogenic type associated with penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN, formerly Bowenoid papulosis and Bowen's disease of the penis) and invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the penis. It is also the most common HPV type in cervical, vulvar, and oropharyngeal carcinomas. Low-risk HPV types 6 and 11 cause condyloma acuminata. High-risk types 16 and 18 account for >70% of cervical cancers.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman with a history of atopic dermatitis is prescribed dupilumab. Which cytokine pathways does dupilumab block?
questions.exp: Dupilumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody that blocks the shared IL-4Rα subunit, thereby inhibiting signaling of both IL-4 and IL-13 - the key Th2 cytokines driving atopic dermatitis. It is approved for moderate-to-severe AD, asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis, and eosinophilic esophagitis. IL-17A/F blockade (secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab) targets psoriasis. IL-12/23 blockade (ustekinumab) targets psoriasis and Crohn's. TNF-alpha blockade (adalimumab) targets many inflammatory conditions.
